# What an Advisor Does for an AI Company

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-advisors-do-ai-companies/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-02-19 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: An advisor helps an AI company decide, introduces it to the people who matter, and tells it which advantages will not last. Scope the relationship in writing, vest the equity, and hire separately for anything that is a job. The market benchmarks are modest: Carta's data puts median pre-seed advisor equity well under 0.25%, typically vesting over two years with a short cliff, and the Founder Institute's standard template ranges from 0.15% to 1% depending on stage and commitment.

## Key points

- An advisor offers pattern recognition for a small amount of equity, a modest fee, or both. They do not run a function, do the work or carry accountability for results.
- The five contributions worth paying for are buyer access, a view on what is durable, commercial translation, regulatory and reputational judgment, and distribution realism.
- Durability matters more in AI than elsewhere: model market share can move by double digits in a year, so an advantage tied to a model is short-lived.
- Structure it in writing: scope, cadence, introductions, vesting with a cliff, a named founder owner and a six-month review.
- Do not ask an advisor to run marketing, manage vendors, write the deck, close deals or be on call. Each is a job.

AI companies accumulate advisors faster than almost any other kind of startup. The category is new, the founders are often technical, investors ask who is around the table, and a well-known name on the deck is cheap to add.

Most of those relationships produce a logo and a quarterly call. A few produce decisions the company would not otherwise have made. The difference is in what the advisor is asked to do.

## What an advisor is

An advisor is a person with relevant experience who helps the founders make better decisions, in exchange for a small amount of equity, a modest fee, or both. The advisor does not run a function, does not do the work, and is not accountable for results. What they offer is pattern recognition: they have seen this decision before, in a company like this, and they know how it tends to go.

That is valuable in AI precisely because so few people have seen the current decisions before. But it also defines the limits. Our comparison of [agencies, consultancies and advisors](https://lowob.com/research/agency-vs-consultancy-vs-advisor/) sets out where advice ends and delivery begins.

| Role | What it provides | Accountable for results | Typical payment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Advisor | Pattern recognition, introductions, judgment on specific decisions | No | Small vested equity, a modest fee, or both |
| Fractional leader | Runs a function part-time | Yes, for that function | Retainer or day rate, sometimes equity |
| Agency or consultancy | Delivers defined work | Yes, for the deliverable | Fee per project or retainer |
| Employee | Does the job full time | Yes | Salary and option grant |

## What a good advisor contributes to an AI company

**Customer and buyer access.** The most valuable advisors introduce the company to the buyers, partners and practitioners who will decide whether it exists in two years. In AI, where trust is the product, one credible introduction can be worth more than a year of outbound. Gartner's May 2026 survey of 645 B2B buyers found 69% preferred to check AI-generated insights with a person; a trusted introduction is the same instinct applied to choosing a vendor.

**A view on what is durable.** Founders close to the technology overestimate how long a capability advantage lasts. An advisor who has watched several model cycles can say which parts of the plan survive the next release and which do not, and push the company toward the workflow, the data and the distribution that persist. The market shows why. Menlo Ventures' 2026 survey found Google's share of enterprise model API spend fell from 21% to 9% in a year while Anthropic's rose from 40% to 55%. Andreessen Horowitz's 2025 CIO survey quoted one buyer saying "for most tasks, all the models perform well enough now." If the models are converging and shares swing that fast, the durable advantage sits elsewhere, as our piece [The model is not the product](https://lowob.com/research/the-model-is-not-the-product/) argues.

**Commercial translation.** Technical founders describe what the model does. Buyers want to know what changes for them. An advisor who has sold into the relevant industry can turn the first into the second, and can tell the company which claims will get it thrown out of a procurement process.

**Regulatory and reputational judgment.** What may be claimed about accuracy and safety, which use cases attract scrutiny, how a data-handling decision will read in eighteen months. This is where an advisor's caution earns its equity. The risk is not theoretical: the US FTC's Operation AI Comply in 2024 targeted companies whose AI claims could not be substantiated, and the SEC fined two investment advisers that year for claiming AI capabilities they did not have. Our explainer on [agent washing](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-washing/) covers the most common overstatement.

**Distribution realism.** Which channels will carry an AI product to its buyer, what that costs, and why the crowded AI advertising auction is the wrong place to start. This is the advice we most often find missing. Our analysis of [why AI companies have a distribution problem disguised as a model problem](https://lowob.com/research/ai-companies-distribution-problem/) sets out the evidence, and our explainer on [go-to-market strategy](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-go-to-market-strategy/) covers the plan an advisor should be pressure-testing.

> The strongest advisor relationships are narrow, structured and used for decisions. The weakest are broad, casual and used for reassurance.

## How the relationship should be structured

A written scope: the topics the advisor covers, the cadence, and the introductions they will attempt. A vesting schedule on any equity, with a cliff, so an advisor who disappears does not keep the grant. A named founder who owns the relationship and prepares for each session with specific decisions rather than an update. A review at six months.

The market norms support a modest grant. Carta's data, published in February 2025, put median pre-seed advisor equity "well under 0.25%", with grants typically vesting over two years with a short cliff, or tied to performance milestones. Companies at that stage typically had one or two advisors. The Founder Institute's Founder Advisor Standard Template (FAST) sets out a widely used grid:

| FAST engagement level | Idea stage | Startup stage | Growth stage |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Standard (monthly meetings) | 0.25% | 0.20% | 0.15% |
| Expert (adds contacts and projects) | 1.00% | 0.80% | 0.60% |

The FAST example vests over two years, with a three-month cliff that lets an unproductive relationship end without any equity changing hands. The Founder Institute also recommends working together for at least a month before discussing terms. An advisor asking for well above these ranges at an early stage is asking to be paid like an executive without the accountability of one.

## What an advisor should not be asked to do

Run marketing. Manage vendors. Write the deck. Close the deal. Be on call. Each of these is a job, and an advisor who takes it on becomes an underpaid, unaccountable employee, which is bad for both sides. When the company needs those things, it should hire them, from a fractional leader, an agency, or a full-time person. Our piece on [the modular GTM team](https://lowob.com/research/the-modular-gtm-team/) covers how to assemble that mix.

| Request | Why it is a job | Who should do it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Run marketing | Needs weekly ownership and a budget | Fractional marketing lead or hire |
| Manage vendors | Needs contracts, follow-up and accountability | Operations lead |
| Write the deck | Needs drafting time and iterations | Founder, with advisor review |
| Close the deal | Needs pipeline ownership and negotiation authority | Founder or sales lead |
| Be on call | Needs availability the equity does not pay for | Nobody, unless contracted |

The strongest advisor relationships are narrow, structured, and used for decisions. The weakest are broad, casual, and used for reassurance.

An advisor helps an AI company decide, introduces it to the people who matter, and tells it which advantages will not last. Scope the relationship in writing, vest the equity, and hire separately for anything that is a job.

## lowob takeaways

- **Pay for pattern recognition.** An advisor offers judgment for a small amount of vested equity, a modest fee, or both, and does not run a function.
- **Ask for the five contributions.** Buyer access, durability, commercial translation, regulatory judgment and distribution realism.
- **Structure it like a contract.** Written scope, vesting with a cliff, a founder owner and a six-month review.
- **Hire for jobs.** Marketing, vendor management, decks, closing and on-call support are jobs.

## Common questions

### What does an advisor do for an AI startup?

Helps the founders make better decisions through pattern recognition: buyer and partner introductions, a view on which advantages are durable, commercial translation, regulatory and reputational judgment, and distribution realism.

### How much equity should a startup advisor get?

Usually less than founders expect. Carta's data puts median pre-seed advisor equity well under 0.25%, and the Founder Institute's FAST template ranges from 0.15% to 1% depending on stage and commitment, typically vesting over two years with a short cliff.

### How should an advisor relationship be structured?

With a written scope covering topics, cadence and introductions, a vesting schedule with a cliff on any equity, a named founder who owns the relationship and brings specific decisions, and a review at six months.

### What should you not ask a startup advisor to do?

Run marketing, manage vendors, write the deck, close the deal or be on call. Each is a job, and an advisor who takes it on becomes an underpaid, unaccountable employee.
